The final submission contains three author classes (EAP, HPL, MWS) with predicted probabilities.

nodes.code_summary: The pipeline implements a Spooky Author Identification solution using: (1) Handcrafted features including stylometric (character ratios, punctuation, word diversity), readability (Flesch, ARI, syllable counts), and POS-approximation features. (2) TF-IDF character n-grams (2-7) and word n-grams (1-3). (3) DeBERTa-v3-large fine-tuning with 5-fold cross-validation, mixup augmentation (two forward passes per batch), label smoothing, and MC dropout inference. (4) XGBoost trained on concatenated stylometric, readability, POS, DeBERTa embeddings, and DeBERTa OOF probabilities. (5) Logistic Regression on sparse n-gram features. (6) Weighted ensemble via a learned logistic regression combiner. The validation metric is multi-class log loss (lower is better).

The primary cause appears to be the mixup augmentation implementation: the code runs two forward passes (original and permuted) per batch without gradient accumulation or memory optimization, effectively doubling memory usage per batch and causing the OOM.

Data preprocessing includes extensive feature engineering: stylometric features (30 features including punctuation ratios, word statistics), readability scores, POS approximation via suffix patterns, TF-IDF character n-grams (2-7), TF-IDF word n-grams (1-3), and punctuation sequence n-grams. Final ensemble uses equal averaging of the three models' probability outputs.

nodes.code_summary: The code implements a three-stage ensemble for the Spooky Author Identification task. Stage 1 (Feature Engineering): extracts stylometric (24 features after variance threshold), readability (4 features), and POS-approximation (5 features) features from text, plus n-gram TF-IDF features (char n-grams 2-7, word n-grams 1-3, punctuation sequences) reduced via chi-squared selection to 10,000 features. Stage 2 (DeBERTa): fine-tunes microsoft/deberta-v3-large with text perturbation augmentation, label smoothing, and early stopping (best at epoch 3). Stage 3 (Ensemble): trains XGBoost and Logistic Regression on engineered features + DeBERTa CLS embeddings, then attempts a learned weighted averaging via a meta LogisticRegression (which fails due to invalid penalty parameter 'none'). Validation metric is multi-class log loss.
nodes.analysis: The execution failed due to an invalid parameter value in the meta-learner LogisticRegression. The code used `penalty='none'` but scikit-learn's LogisticRegression only accepts `{'l2', 'elasticnet', 'l1'}` or None (not the string 'none'). This caused a `InvalidParameterError` before any ensemble could be evaluated. The DeBERTa fine-tuning completed (best val loss: 0.4355 at epoch 3), XGBoost achieved a validation log loss of 0.3124, and Logistic Regression achieved 0.5168, but the ensemble stage crashed.

nodes.code_summary: The code implements an ensemble approach for author identification combining handcrafted stylometric features (stylometrics, readability, POS approximation), TF-IDF n-gram features (character and word), punctuation sequence features, and DeBERTa-v3-large embeddings. A DeBERTa model is fine-tuned for sequence classification. XGBoost and Logistic Regression classifiers are trained on the extracted features and embeddings. An ensemble weight optimization is performed using logistic regression on the validation predictions from the three models to produce the final submission.

The simplest fix is to remove the duplicate and broken CV sections, keep only the single split approach, and ensure all dependencies are defined before use.
nodes.code_summary: The code implements a two-model ensemble for authorship attribution. Data preprocessing includes loading train/test CSVs and label encoding authors. Feature engineering extracts 39 handcrafted stylometric features (basic stats, punctuation ratios, POS approximation, readability scores, vocabulary-based features using archaic/emotional/Lovecraft word lists). N-gram features are extracted using CountVectorizers at character (2-7) and word (1-2) levels, plus punctuation sequences. The primary model is DeBERTa-v3-large fine-tuned for sequence classification (3 classes) with AdamW optimizer, linear warmup scheduler, and mixed precision training. A Logistic Regression classifier is trained on the sparse n-gram features. The final predictions are a weighted blend (0.80 DeBERTa, 0.20 LR) optimized on the validation set. nodes.code_summary: The code implements a comprehensive ensemble for Spooky Author Identification. It extracts handcrafted stylometric (26 dims), readability (4 dims), and POS-approximation (5 dims) features, plus TF-IDF character/word n-grams (13,500 dims). It fine-tunes DeBERTa-v3-large with 5-fold cross-validation, layer-wise learning rate decay, gradient accumulation, and cosine schedule. OOF predictions and final-layer CLS embeddings are extracted. An XGBoost classifier is trained on concatenated dense features (stylo + readability + POS + embeddings + DeBERTa OOF probs), and a Logistic Regression is trained on sparse n-gram features. A weighted ensemble (DeBERTa + XGB + LR) is optimized via grid search on a holdout validation set.

The final validation metric is effectively meaningless due to this numerical instability.

nodes.code_summary: The pipeline loads the Spooky Author Identification dataset with 3 authors and performs a single stratified 80/20 train-validation split. Text is tokenized using the DeBERTa-v3-large tokenizer with max length 512. The model architecture consists of a DeBERTa-v3-large encoder followed by a 2-layer BiLSTM, an attention layer, and a classifier head. Training uses AdamW optimizer with linear warmup scheduling, gradient clipping, mixed precision (AMP), and label smoothing loss. Early stopping with patience 4 monitors validation log loss. A logistic regression meta-classifier is trained on the validation set predictions to perform learned soft voting ensemble, and final test predictions are generated and saved as a CSV submission.

nodes.code_summary: The pipeline implements a multi-model ensemble for the Spooky Author Identification task. It extracts handcrafted stylometric features (30-dim), readability scores (4-dim), POS tag approximations (5-dim), and n-gram features (character and word TF-IDF). A DeBERTa-v3-large model is fine-tuned with R-Drop (double forward pass with KL divergence) and label smoothing using 5-fold cross-validation. DeBERTa embeddings are extracted via mean pooling of the last hidden layer. An XGBoost classifier is trained on the concatenation of handcrafted features, DeBERTa embeddings, and OOF meta-features. A sparse logistic regression is trained on the TF-IDF n-gram features. The three models are ensembled via grid-search weighted averaging on the holdout validation set, optimizing for multi-class log loss.

nodes.code_summary: The script implements a multi-stage ensemble for Spooky Author Identification (3 authors: EAP, HPL, MWS). Stage 1 extracts stylometric features (archaic/emotional word ratios, punctuation, readability indices, POS approximations), n-gram TF-IDF vectors (char/word/punctuation) with chi-squared feature selection. Finally, ensemble weights are optimized via grid search on validation log loss. Validation uses stratified 90/10 split with multi-class log loss as the evaluation metric.

nodes.code_summary: The pipeline implements a multi-model ensemble for the Spooky Author Identification task. Preprocessing includes extraction of stylometric features (30 dims, reduced via variance threshold), readability features (4 dims), POS approximation features (5 dims), and TF-IDF character/word n-grams (13,500 sparse features). DeBERTa-v3-large is fine-tuned using 5-fold cross-validation with label smoothing and MC Dropout for OOF predictions. nodes.plan: Looking at the error, I can see two main issues: 1. **Duplicate code**: The DeBERTa training is defined twice - first with the custom attention pooling model (which crashes), then again with the standard model. This makes the code redundant and causes the crash. 2. **einsum error in custom model**: The `layer_weights` tensor shape is wrong for the einsum operation. Execution results show severe overfitting: DeBERTa validation loss increases after epoch 2-3 (e.g., fold 1: 0.416\u21920.713), while train loss continues to drop (0.332\u21920.079). This matches historical failed experiments where MixUp and MC Dropout worsened performance. Historical successful experiments used 5-fold CV, mean pooling, lower learning rate (8e-6), and removed MixUp/label smoothing to achieve better generalization. Therefore, the refinement should: (1) in `model_design`, remove MixUp and label smoothing, add mean pooling for embeddings, and use lower LR; (2) in `training_evaluation`, implement 5-fold CV with averaged predictions, reduce epochs to 5 with low...
nodes.code_summary: The solution uses a multi-stage ensemble for author attribution. Stage 1 extracts handcrafted features (30 stylometric, 4 readability, 5 POS-approximation) plus character/word n-grams and punctuation sequences. Stage 2 fine-tunes a DeBERTa-v3-large with 5-fold cross-validation (1e-5 LR, 5 epochs, AMP), extracting mean-pooled embeddings and fold-averaged probabilities. Stage 3 trains XGBoost on combined handcrafted + embedding features. Stage 4 trains multinomial logistic regression on sparse n-gram features. Stage 5 learns ensemble weights via a logistic regression meta-learner (no penalty) on stacked model probabilities. The final submission averages DeBERTa (CV), XGBoost, and LR predictions using learned weights.
nodes.analysis: The code executed successfully within the 6-hour time limit (completing in 3 hours). The pipeline performed 5-fold cross-validation fine-tuning of a DeBERTa-v3-large model, followed by XGBoost and Logistic Regression training on handcrafted and embedding features, with a final ensemble. nodes.plan: Looking at the error, the issue is in Stage 2 fine-tuning. The error "Trying to backward through the graph a second time" occurs because: 1. `gradient_checkpointing_enable()` is enabled but the model was already loaded from a checkpoint and used in eval mode before Stage 2. The gradient checkpointing creates a wrapper that re-runs forward during backward, and this conflicts with the model's state. 2. The root cause is that gradient checkpointing should be enabled BEFORE any forward pass, not after loading state_dict and re-enabling. The fix: Remove gradient checkpointing entirely (it's not necessary for our batch size) and instead reduce memory by adjusting batch size or enabling it properly at model initialization. nodes.code_summary: The code implements a multi-model ensemble for author attribution (3 authors: EAP, HPL, MWS). It uses: (1) A custom DebertaV3ForSequenceClassification model with attention pooling over the last 4 hidden layers (with learned per-layer weights), trained via 5-fold cross-validation; (2) Standard DeBERTa fine-tuning also with 5-fold CV; (3) Hand-crafted feature extraction including stylometric features, readability metrics, POS tag approximations, TF-IDF character/word n-grams, and punctuation sequences; (4) XGBoost classifier trained on combined embeddings + hand-crafted features; (5) Logistic Regression trained on TF-IDF sparse features; (6) An ensemble that learns optimal weights via logistic regression over the three model outputs. The submission file is generated by blending all three models with learned weights.

nodes.code_summary: The code implements a complete pipeline for the Spooky Author Identification task. Data preprocessing includes text cleaning and tokenization. Feature engineering extracts stylometric features (30 dims), readability metrics (Flesch, ARI), POS tag approximations, and character/word n-gram TF-IDF features. The model architecture includes: (1) DeBERTa-v3-large fine-tuned with 5-fold cross-validation and early stopping, (2) XGBoost classifier trained on DeBERTa embeddings + handcrafted features + OOF probabilities, and (3) Logistic Regression on sparse n-gram features. These are combined via a learned logistic regression ensemble. Validation uses stratified hold-out (90/10 split) with multi-class log loss as the evaluation metric.

nodes.code_summary: The code implements a complete pipeline for the Spooky Author Identification task. It loads training and test data, extracts handcrafted stylometric (26 dims), readability (4 dims), and POS approximation (5 dims) features, as well as TF-IDF character/word n-gram and punctuation sequence features. It fine-tunes a DeBERTa-v3-large model with 5-fold cross-validation, using AdamW optimizer with linear warmup, label smoothing via cross-entropy, and mixed-precision training. DeBERTa embeddings (mean pooled) are extracted from the last fold's model. An XGBoost classifier is trained on the dense features combined with DeBERTa OOF probabilities as meta-features, and a Logistic Regression classifier is trained on the sparse n-gram features. Finally, a weighted ensemble (DeBERTa, XGBoost, LR) is optimized via grid search on a holdout validation set to minimize multi-class log loss.
nodes.analysis: The pipeline executed successfully within the 6-hour time limit, completing 5-fold cross-validation on DeBERTa-v3-large, XGBoost, and Logistic Regression training, followed by an ensemble weight grid search. The final optimized ensemble achieved a validation log loss of approximately 0.3254, with DeBERTa contributing the most weight. All models trained without errors and a submission file was generated.

The code implements a document denoising solution using a U-Net architecture with a frozen DINOv2 (ViT-S/14) encoder. Images are resized to 540x540, normalized with ImageNet statistics, and augmented with random horizontal flips. The fix: Change the indexing from `gray.shape[2]`, `gray.shape[3]` to `gray.shape[1]`, `gray.shape[2]` since `gray` is a 3D tensor `[1, H, W]`.

nodes.plan: Looking at the error trace, the issue is in the `NAFBlock` class. The `SimpleGate` splits channels in half, but the subsequent `conv2` expects `dw_channel` (which is `c * DW_Expand = 32*2 = 64`) after gating, not `c`. However, after `SimpleGate` which halves the channels, `dw_channel` becomes `c * DW_Expand / 2`, but `conv2` is defined with input channels = `dw_channel` (64). The issue is that `SimpleGate` halves the channels from `dw_channel * 2` (128) to `dw_channel` (64), and then `conv2` expects 64 channels. But in the SCA branch, `x * self.sca(x)` requires `x` to have `c` channels (32), while `x` actually has `dw_channel` (64) channels after gating and before `conv2`. The fix is to ensure the SCA block operates on the correct channel dimension — we need to add a down-projection before the SCA or restructure the block. Alternatively, simpler fix: change the `sca` to use a `Conv2d`...

nodes.code_summary: The code implements a Denoising Attention U-Net for image denoising on the Denoising Dirty Documents dataset. Data preprocessing involves loading grayscale images and extracting overlapping patches of size 128x128 with stride 64. The model architecture is a U-Net with attention gates, GroupNorm, SiLU activations, and transposed convolutions (bilinear=False). nodes.plan: Looking at the error trace, I can identify the root cause clearly: **Root Cause**: During test inference with TTA, when the test images are padded to multiples of 14, the padded dimensions may still not produce a perfect square grid of patches (e.g., 34×34 = 1156 patches, but the actual number of patches from DINOv2 is 449280/384 = 1170 patches = 34.21 × 34.21 → not square). The `grid_size = int(np.sqrt(N))` assumes a perfect square, but the actual feature map from DINOv2 has `ceil(H/14) * ceil(W/14)` patches, which may not be square if the input was padded to a rectangle (not a square). **Fix**: During test inference, we must either: 1. Pad the image to a square size (so patch grid is guaranteed square), OR 2. Use the actual grid dimensions from the forward pass instead of assuming a square. nodes.code_summary: The code implements a DINOv2-based U-Net for document denoising. Data preprocessing includes multi-scale resizing (420, 546, 672), random brightness/contrast adjustment, Gaussian noise injection, random erasing, and random horizontal flips. Images are normalized using ImageNet statistics. The model uses a DINOv2 ViT-S/14 encoder (trainable) with a convolutional decoder featuring skip connections, up-convolutions, and a final sigmoid output. Loss is a combined L1 + DSSIM + edge-aware Sobel loss. Validation uses RMSE as the metric. Training employs AdamW optimizer with differential learning rates (encoder warmup to 5e-5, decoder at 1e-3), cosine annealing scheduler, mixed precision training, and early stopping (patience=10).

nodes.code_summary: The code implements a SwinIR-based image denoising model for the Denoising Dirty Documents competition. Data preprocessing loads grayscale images, pads them to multiples of window_size, and resizes to 256x256 for consistent batching. Data augmentation includes flips, rotations, contrast jitter, and brightness shift. The model architecture is SwinIR with shallow feature extraction via Conv2d, deep feature extraction via Residual Swin Transformer Groups (RSTB) with window attention and cyclic shifts, and reconstruction via Conv2d with global residual and sigmoid output. Training uses L1 loss, AdamW optimizer, cosine annealing LR scheduler, mixed precision (AMP), gradient clipping, and early stopping. Validation metric is RMSE (lower is better). Test inference uses patch-based reconstruction with stride 64 and linear blending weight map.

nodes.code_summary: The code implements a NAFNet-based image denoising pipeline for a Kaggle competition. Data preprocessing: images are resized to 256x256 and overlapping patches (64x64 and 128x128) are extracted with strides. Curriculum learning is employed: training starts with large patches (128x128) for 10 epochs, then switches to small patches (64x64). The model is a NAFNet denoiser with multi-scale feature fusion (a main branch and a downsampled global context branch), using NAFBlocks with depthwise convolutions and gating but no nonlinear activations. Training uses mixed precision (AMP), L1+L2 combined loss, AdamW optimizer with cosine annealing warm restarts and warmup. Validation involves reconstructing full images from overlapping patches by averaging predictions, then computing RMSE. Test inference similarly reconstructs denoised images from small patches for submission.

nodes.code_summary: Data preprocessing: Images are loaded as grayscale, resized to 256×256, normalized to [0,1], and split into overlapping 64×64 patches with stride 32. Patches are split by image ID into train/validation sets (85/15 split). Augmentation: Random horizontal flips and ±5° rotations applied online via a custom dataset class. Model: A simplified NAFNet (no downsampling) with 6 NAFBlocks (using LayerNorm, depthwise convolutions, and gating) and ~47K parameters, with a Sigmoid output. Training: Combined L1+L2 loss (0.3/0.7 weights), AdamW optimizer, cosine annealing warm restarts with 5-epoch linear warmup, mixed precision (AMP), early stopping, and validation RMSE computed by reconstructing full images from overlapping patch predictions. Inference: Overlapping patches are reconstructed via averaging, resized to original dimensions, and saved as pixel-level CSV submission.

nodes.plan: The issue is clear: the DINOv3 backbone loading via torch.hub.load fails because the expected hubconf.py file and checkpoint structure are not found at `/kaggle/input/dinov3/`. Since we cannot rely on external model download or specific Kaggle dataset paths, we need to use a **standard CNN-based autoencoder architecture** that does not depend on external weights. Let me fix this by replacing the DINOv3-dependent model with a standard U-Net architecture that can be trained from scratch, which is both robust and performs well for denoising tasks.
nodes.code_summary: Data loading: images resized to 256x256 grayscale and normalized to [0,1]. Train/validation split by image ID (85/15 ratio). Model: U-Net autoencoder with encoder-decoder architecture, batch normalization, ReLU activations, and sigmoid output. Skip connections with interpolation to handle size mismatches. Training: combined L1+L2 loss (0.3/0.7 weights), AdamW optimizer, cosine annealing LR scheduler, mixed precision training, early stopping (patience-based when val RMSE exceeds 1.05x best). Validation metric: RMSE. Submission: pixel-level predictions written as (id, value) rows.

Since we cannot rely on external model download or specific Kaggle dataset paths, we need to use a **standard CNN-based autoencoder architecture** that does not depend on external weights. Let me fix this by replacing the DINOv3-dependent model with a standard U-Net architecture that can be trained from scratch, which is both robust and performs well for denoising tasks.
Data loading: images resized to 256x256 grayscale and normalized to [0,1]. Train/validation split by image ID (85/15 ratio). Model: U-Net autoencoder with encoder-decoder architecture, batch normalization, ReLU activations, and sigmoid output. Skip connections with interpolation to handle size mismatches. Training: combined L1+L2 loss (0.3/0.7 weights), AdamW optimizer, cosine annealing LR scheduler, mixed precision training, early stopping (patience-based when val RMSE exceeds 1.05x best). Validation metric: RMSE. Submission: pixel-level predictions written as (id, value) rows.
The code executed successfully, completing training over 12 epochs (with early stopping triggered at epoch 12). The best validation RMSE achieved was 0.136197, and the model was used to generate a submission CSV with pixel-level predictions for 29 test images. No errors or bugs were encountered during execution.

nodes.code_summary: The code implements a denoising attention U-Net for image restoration. Data preprocessing involves extracting overlapping patches (128x128 with stride 64) from grayscale images normalized to [0,1]. Training uses heavy augmentation including flips, rotations, brightness/contrast jitter, and Gaussian noise. The model architecture features a U-Net with double convolution blocks, group normalization, SiLU activations, attention gates in skip connections, and dropout in the bottleneck. Training uses a combined loss (RMSE + SSIM + edge loss) with AdamW optimizer, cosine annealing warm restarts scheduler, mixed precision training (AMP), and early stopping. Validation uses RMSE as the primary metric. Test inference reconstructs full images via overlapping patches with linear ramp blending weights.

nodes.plan: Looking at the error, the problem is in the `SwinTransformerBlock.forward()` method. The input resolution is 256x256, but when the window partitioning/collapse happens, there's a shape mismatch in the residual path because `H` and `W` get changed during the forward pass but the `shortcut` still holds the original shape. This is caused by wrong handling of input resolution vs actual tensor dimensions after the norm1 reshape. The root issue: After `x = self.norm1(x)` which expects [B, L, C] shape, then `x = x.transpose(1, 2).view(B, C, H, W)` reconstructs the 2D shape. But `view` requires `H * W` to exactly match `L`. After padding and window merging, the shape could be different from original `H, W`, causing dimension mismatch in the final residual add. Let me fix the SwinIR architecture to use a simpler and more robust approach - a standard UNet-like convolutional autoencoder with res...
nodes.code_summary: The code implements a denoising autoencoder for dirty document images using a Nested Attention U-Net with channel and spatial attention blocks. Data is loaded from PNG images, padded to window-size multiples, and resized to 256x256 for training with augmentations (flips, rotations, contrast/brightness jitter). The U-Net has 4 encoder/decoder levels with 32 base features, bottleneck at 512 channels, and uses ConvBlocks with batch normalization, residual connections, and attention. A global residual skip connection (1x1 conv) from input to output is added. Training uses L1 loss, AdamW optimizer with cosine annealing LR scheduler, mixed precision (AMP), gradient clipping, and early stopping with 15 patience. Validation uses RMSE. Test inference uses patch-based reconstruction with overlapping 128x64 patches and linear blending weights.

nodes.plan: Looking at the error, the issue is clear: `self.base_filters` is used in the `forward` method but was never saved as an instance attribute in `__init__`. The fix is to add `self.base_filters = base_filters` in the constructor. Additionally, there are other SEBlock instances in the forward method that use `self.base_filters * 8`, `self.base_filters * 4`, etc. which will also fail without this fix.
nodes.code_summary: The code implements a patch-based image denoising U-Net for the Denoising Dirty Documents competition. Data preprocessing: extracts overlapping 64x32 patches from grayscale images, computes a noise prior (residual from median filtering) as a second input channel, and applies augmentation (flips, rotation). Model architecture: a 4-level U-Net with Gaussian noise injection, Squeeze-and-Excitation blocks, dropout, and skip connections, using 2 input channels (noisy image + noise prior) and 1 output channel (denoised image). Training uses a combined MSE + (1-SSIM) loss, AdamW optimizer with OneCycleLR scheduler, gradient clipping, and early stopping. Validation uses RMSE as the metric. Test inference applies TTA (horizontal/vertical flips) and reconstructs full images via weighted averaging of overlapping patches.

nodes.plan: Looking at the error, the root cause is in the multi-scale TTA test inference section. During test time, `F.interpolate` on the input image produces float32 tensors, but after `autocast()` the encoder's convolution expects half precision (float16 due to AMP). The issue is that `dirty` tensor is float32 and `normalize` keeps it float32, but after `autocast()` the first convolution in DINOv2's patch embedding has its bias in half precision while input is float32. The fix is to ensure the input tensor dtype is aligned with the model's dtype (half when using AMP autocast, float otherwise). Additionally, I notice the submission file will be ~5.8 million rows, which is correct. nodes.code_summary: The code implements a document denoising pipeline using a DINOv2-based U-Net architecture. Training images are preprocessed with multi-scale resizing (420, 546, 672), random flips, brightness/contrast adjustments, Gaussian noise, and random erasing augmentation. The model uses a DINOv2 ViT-S/14 encoder (trainable with linear warmup) coupled with a convolutional decoder with skip connections from intermediate transformer blocks. A combined loss function is used (L1 + DSSIM + edge-aware Sobel loss). Training uses AdamW with differential learning rates, mixed precision (GradScaler), cosine annealing LR scheduling, early stopping, and validation RMSE as the tracking metric. Test-time augmentation with multi-scale inference (420, 546, 672) is applied.

nodes.code_summary: The implementation uses a U-Net architecture with a frozen DINOv2 (ViT-S/14) encoder for document denoising. Data preprocessing resizes images to 546x546 and applies random cropping with ColorJitter augmentation. A progressive resolution curriculum increases crop size from 196 to 392 over training. The decoder uses multi-scale dilated convolution blocks with channel attention (SE). Training uses mixed precision with CombinedLoss (L1 + DSSIM), AdamW optimizer with differential learning rates, cosine annealing scheduler, and warmup before unfreezing the last 4 encoder blocks. Validation uses RMSE as the metric, and test predictions use a sliding window with 50% overlap for full-image reconstruction.

nodes.code_summary: The code implements a multi-scale patch-based image denoising pipeline for a Kaggle competition. Data preprocessing: loads grayscale images (420x540) and extracts overlapping patches at three scales (64x64, 128x128, 256x256). Feature engineering: patches are extracted with strides and aggregated across scales. Model architecture: a SimpleUNet with Squeeze-and-Excitation blocks and a MultiScaleFusion module in the bottleneck, taking 2 input channels (noisy patch + scale label). Training uses a combined loss (L1 + VGG perceptual loss), AdamW optimizer with cosine annealing scheduler, and early stopping with patience 15. Validation uses RMSE on reconstructed full images by aggregating overlapping patch predictions with weighted averaging.

The `_pad_to_multiple` function pads to multiples of 32, but since rotation changes the image size differently per image, the tensors end up with different shapes and can't be batched. The fix is to apply deterministic cropping or resizing to ensure all images in a batch have the same dimensions. I'll modify the dataset to resize all images to a fixed size after augmentation to ensure consistent tensor shapes for batching.
nodes.code_summary: The code implements a document denoising solution using a NAFNet (Non-linear Activation Free Network) architecture. Data preprocessing loads grayscale images, converts to RGB for augmentations (horizontal flip, rotation, color jitter), resizes to fixed 544x544, and normalizes pixel values to [0,1]. The model uses a U-Net-like encoder-decoder with NAFBlocks containing SimpleGate and simplified channel attention. Training uses Charbonnier loss, AdamW optimizer with cosine annealing scheduler, mixed precision training, and early stopping with patience of 10 epochs. The validation metric is RMSE on a 15% holdout split.

nodes.plan: ## Plan The root cause is numerical instability during training: the CombinedLoss computes a Fourier loss using `torch.log(torch.abs(fft))` which can produce `-inf` or NaN when magnitudes are zero, causing the entire loss to explode. Additionally, the SSIM loss uses a Gaussian kernel constructed manually but not correctly normalized per group, and the CosineAnnealingWarmRestarts scheduler is stepped every batch which is incorrect — it should be stepped per epoch for proper restarts. The edge loss Sobel kernels can also produce large gradients. **Fix strategy:** 1. Replace the CombinedLoss with a simpler, numerically stable loss: RMSE + SSIM (using a standard PyTorch implementation) — remove Fourier loss (which causes inf/nan) and edge loss (unnecessary complexity). 2. Fix scheduler stepping: move `scheduler.step()` to per-epoch (before or after validation) instead of per-batch. 3. Red...
nodes.code_summary: The code implements an image denoising solution using a multi-scale attention U-Net with channel attention (SE blocks) and attention gates. PatchExtractionDataset extracts overlapping 128x128 patches with stride 64/128 for train/val, applying heavy data augmentation (flips, rotations, contrast jitter, brightness shift, Gaussian noise, CutOut). The model uses DoubleConv blocks with GroupNorm and SiLU activation, a 5-level U-Net with bilinear upsampling, and outputs sigmoid activations. Training uses a combined RMSE + SSIM loss, AdamW optimizer with differential learning rates (backbone 5e-4, head 1e-3), cosine annealing warm restarts scheduler, mixed precision (AMP), gradient clipping, and early stopping with patience 15. Test inference reconstructs full images using weighted blending of overlapping patches with a linear ramp weight map.

The training dataloader never adds the noise prior channel to the dirty patches, so when the model tries to run `forward` with 3-channel input, it fails at the convolution layer which expects 4 channels. **Fix Strategy**: 1. In `PatchDenoisingDataset.__getitem__`, after creating the dirty patch tensor, compute a noise prior channel (using `_compute_noise_prior` logic adapted for patches) and concatenate it as a 4th channel. 2. Update the validation path similarly to ensure consistency. 3. Ensure the test dataset already handles the 4th channel (it does — it adds a dummy noise prior).

Data augmentation includes synthetic artifacts (blotches, streaks, shading), brightness/contrast adjustments, Gaussian noise, and random erasing. The loss function is a combined L1 + DSSIM + edge-aware loss. Validation uses RMSE as the metric. The encoder receives a linear warmup learning rate schedule while the decoder trains at higher LR. Test-time augmentation is applied at 3 scales (420, 546, 672) with multi-scale averaging.

nodes.code_summary: The code implements an image denoising task using a Multi-Scale Attention U-Net. Data preprocessing: loads grayscale images (dirty/clean pairs) resized to 256x256 with normalization to [0,1], and applies augmentation (horizontal flips, small rotations). Model architecture: a U-Net with double convolution blocks (GroupNorm + SiLU), attention gates in the up-sampling path, and a sigmoid output. Validation strategy: 85/15 train/validation split, early stopping with patience 15, evaluates pixel-wise RMSE.

nodes.plan: Looking at the error, the root cause is clear: `num_epochs` is used in the `OneCycleLR` scheduler definition but is defined later in the code. This is a simple ordering issue — the variable must be defined before it's used. The fix: Move the `num_epochs = 50` definition above the scheduler initialization.
nodes.code_summary: The code loads grayscale images (noisy and clean) and extracts overlapping 64x64 patches with stride 32, applying data augmentation (flips, rotations) on training patches. A U-Net autoencoder with Squeeze-and-Excitation blocks, Gaussian noise injection, dropout, and batch normalization is used as the denoising model. Training uses a combined loss (70% MSE + 30% 1-SSIM) with AdamW optimizer and OneCycleLR scheduler, gradient clipping, and early stopping based on validation RMSE. Test images are denoised patch-wise and reconstructed via weighted averaging of overlapping predictions.

Uses a DenoisingDataset that loads grayscale images, normalizes to [0,1], and applies data augmentation (random flips, slight rotations). Training uses a CombinedLoss (RMSE + SSIM + edge loss), AdamW optimizer with differential learning rates (backbone: 1e-3, head: 1e-2), CosineAnnealingWarmRestarts scheduler, and mixed precision via GradScaler. Data loading involves loading images, padding to window-size multiples, and resizing to 256x256 with augmentations (flips, rotations, contrast/brightness jitter). The SwinIR architecture uses convolutional embedding, multiple Residual Swin Transformer Groups (RSTBs) with window attention, and a residual reconstruction head. The F.conv2d inside ssim() then fails because the input (HalfTensor) and the window weight (FloatTensor) have different types. nodes.code_summary: The code implements a U-Net style denoising model using a frozen DINOv2 ViT-S/14 encoder. It loads 115 training and 29 test PNG images, resizes them to 546x546, and applies random cropping with progressive resolution (196→294→392). nodes.code_summary: The code implements a denoising autoencoder for the Denoising Dirty Documents competition. nodes.plan: I'll analyze the bug and provide a fix. **Root Cause**: The error occurs because `test_image_sizes[img_id]` stores the image size as `img.size` which returns `(width, height)` from PIL. Then in the test inference loop, `orig_w, orig_h = test_image_sizes[img_id]` is correct, but later `h, w = test_image_sizes[img_id][1], test_image_sizes[img_id][0]` flips this ordering, causing `cv2.resize` to receive invalid dimensions. The actual crash happens because `output_np[i, 0]` has shape `(256, 256)` from the model resize during test dataset creation, but `cv2.resize` expects a valid interpolation function which fails when the target size is 0 or negative. **Fix**: Correct the dimension ordering in the submission creation section and ensure `cv2.resize` receives the proper dimensions `(orig_w, orig_h)` for width first.

nodes.code_summary: The code implements a DINOv2-based U-Net for document denoising. Data preprocessing: loads grayscale images, resizes to 546×546, normalizes to [0,1], converts to 3-channel inputs with random horizontal flip augmentation. nodes.plan: Looking at the error, the root cause is clear: The `MultiScaleBlock` outputs have `out_channels * 4` channels (since it concatenates 4 dilation branches, each producing `out_channels`), but the subsequent transposed convolution layers expect `out_channels` channels. For example: - `self.up4` expects 128 channels but gets 512 (128 * 4) from `msb4` - `self.up3` expects 64 channels but gets 512 from `msb3` (since `msb4` output 128*4=512 → up4 reduces to 128 → `msb4` outputs 128*4=512 → up3 expects 128) The fix is to reduce the MultiScaleBlock's output channels by 4x (divide by the number of branches) so that the concatenation produces the desired channel count.
nodes.code_summary: The code implements a document denoising solution using a DINOv2 encoder (small ViT) with a U-Net style decoder featuring multi-scale dilated convolutional blocks with channel attention (SE). Data preprocessing includes resizing images to 546x546, converting to RGB, and applying random crops with color jitter augmentation. Training uses mixed precision (AMP), a combined L1 + DSSIM loss, progressive resolution curriculum (196→294→392 crop sizes), cosine annealing warm restarts scheduler, and early stopping. Validation evaluates RMSE, and test inference uses a sliding window approach with 50% overlap for full-image reconstruction.

The final submission file was generated with 8,645,364 rows.

nodes.plan: I merged the three pipeline steps into a coherent script, resolving conflicts between the feature engineering approach (pixel-level features) and the model design (image-to-image CNN). Since the model expects full images as input, I kept the image loading from step 3 and removed the pixel-level feature engineering from step 1 that was incompatible. I also added a DINOv3 baseline branch as required, fixed the combined loss to use RMSE as the evaluation metric, and ensured consistent preprocessing between validation and test inference.
nodes.code_summary: The code loads grayscale image pairs (noisy/clean) from directories, resizes them to 256x256, splits by image ID (15% validation), and trains a denoising model. The model uses a frozen DINOv3 ViT-L/16 backbone to extract patch tokens, projects them via MLP to a spatial feature map, then decodes with ConvTranspose2d layers back to full resolution with a Sigmoid output. Training uses combined L1+L2 loss, AdamW optimizer, cosine annealing LR scheduler, mixed precision, and early stopping, with validation RMSE as the evaluation metric.

nodes.code_summary: The code implements a U-Net for image denoising (grayscale). Data: 115 training images, 18 validation (15% split), 29 test images. Preprocessing uses PIL images with transforms (RandomHorizontalFlip for train, ToTensor for eval). The custom DenoisingDataset attempts to apply identical random transforms to noisy/clean pairs using manual torch seed manipulation. Model: a standard U-Net with 4 encoder/decoder blocks (64-128-256-512 features), bottleneck, skip connections, and sigmoid output. Loss: combined MSE + L1 + total variation loss. Optimizer: AdamW with CosineAnnealingLR, mixed precision training, early stopping with patience=10 for 50 epochs. Validation metric: RMSE.

nodes.plan: Looking at the error, the issue is clear: `extract_patches_multi_scale` returns a list of lists (one per scale), but the code is unpacking it incorrectly. When called with `[PATCH_SIZE_MEDIUM]` and `[STRIDE_MEDIUM]` (single-element lists), it returns: - `test_patches` = `[array_of_medium_patches]` → `test_patches[0]` is the actual array - `positions` = `[list_of_positions]` → `positions[0]` is the actual list of tuples - `scales` = `[list_of_scales]` → `scales[0]` is the actual list But the code loops over `test_patches[0]` (the patches array) and then tries `positions[p_idx]` which indexes into the outer list, not the inner list of positions. It should be `positions[0][p_idx]`.
nodes.code_summary: The code implements a denoising autoencoder for dirty document images. Data preprocessing extracts overlapping multi-scale patches (64x64, 128x128, 256x256) from training images and uses a scale-aware input (noisy patch concatenated with a scale mask). The model is a U-Net with Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) blocks, multi-scale fusion at the bottleneck, and a VGG-based perceptual loss combined with L1 loss. Validation is performed by reconstructing full images from overlapping 128x128 patches with weighted averaging, and evaluation uses RMSE. Augmentations include flips, rotations, brightness/contrast changes, noise, random erasing, and elastic deformation. Training uses AdamW optimizer, cosine annealing scheduler, and mixed precision (AMP).

nodes.code_summary: The code implements an end-to-end binary classification pipeline for cactus detection using images. It loads labeled image data, creates a stratified train/validation split (85/15), and builds a custom dataset with data augmentation (random flips, rotation, color jitter) for training and standard transforms for validation. The model uses a pretrained EfficientNet-B0 backbone from timm with a custom classification head (adaptive pooling, dropout, linear layer). Training employs Focal Loss (gamma=2.0, alpha=0.75) to handle class imbalance, AdamW optimizer, cosine annealing LR scheduling, and mixed precision training. Validation uses ROC-AUC as the metric with early stopping (patience=5). The best model is saved and used for test inference and submission generation.

Data preprocessing includes resizing to 224x224, RandAugment for training-time augmentation, and standard ImageNet normalization. nodes.code_summary: The code implements a binary classification pipeline for aerial cactus identification. Data: stratified train/val split (85/15) from a CSV; images resized to 256x256 with augmentation (flips, rotation, color jitter) and SigLIP-style normalization (mean=0.5, std=0.5). Model: loads a pretrained SigLIP2 vision-language model (google/siglip2-so400m-patch16-256) from HuggingFace transformers, freezes the backbone, and adds a custom classifier head (LayerNorm → Dropout → Linear → GELU → BatchNorm → Dropout → Linear → Dropout → Linear). Training: BCEWithLogitsLoss, AdamW optimizer, CosineAnnealingLR scheduler, mixed-precision (GradScaler), early stopping with patience 7. Validation: ROC AUC metric; test-time augmentation (horizontal flip averaging). The bug is that the SigLIP2 model requires both image and text inputs (input_ids) but only pixel_values are passed.
nodes.analysis: The execution failed due to a bug in the SigLIP2 model forward pass. The error occurred because the model's backbone (AutoModel for "google/siglip2-so400m-patch16-256") expects both pixel_values and input_ids (as it is a multimodal vision-language model), but only pixel_values were provided, causing a ValueError: "You have to specify input_ids". The training loop crashed at the first batch of the first epoch, so no validation metric was obtained.

This crashes the entire script before training can even begin. The fix is to replace the DINOv3 feature extraction with a standard, readily available pretrained model from `torchvision` (like ResNet or EfficientNet) that can be loaded without any external files. This ensures the code runs in any environment without dependency on specific checkpoint files.
nodes.code_summary: The pipeline loads image data and extracts a comprehensive set of handcrafted features including color histograms, GLCM texture features, LBP features, edge features, statistical features, HOG features, and pooled grayscale features. These are combined with CNN features extracted from a pretrained EfficientNet-V2-S model. The features are standardized and concatenated, then used to train a simple MLP classifier with BatchNorm, ReLU, and Dropout layers. Validation uses a single StratifiedKFold split with early stopping based on ROC AUC, and the best model is saved for test inference.

nodes.code_summary: The code implements an end-to-end fine-tuning approach using EfficientNet-B0 as a backbone with a custom MLP classifier head for binary classification (cactus vs. no cactus). Data preprocessing includes image resizing to 224x224, RandAugment for training augmentation, and standard normalization. A stratified K-fold split is used for validation. The model uses separate learning rates (5e-5 for backbone, 1e-3 for head), CutMix augmentation, label smoothing BCE loss, gradient clipping, and a warmup + cosine annealing warm restarts scheduler. Training employs mixed precision (AMP) and early stopping with patience of 7.

nodes.plan: The bug is a **shared memory (shm) exhaustion** issue when using DataLoader with `num_workers>0` and `pin_memory=True`. The DINOv2 model processes images at 518x518, which are large tensors, and with 4 workers each holding copies of data in shared memory, the system's `/dev/shm` gets overwhelmed. The fix is to set `num_workers=0` to avoid multiprocessing shared memory entirely, and set `pin_memory=False`. Additionally, we need to fix a bug in the classifier forward pass where `nn.GELU()` is called as a function on tensor `h` but it's not instantiated as a module—this will crash at the second forward pass. We should replace it with `F.gelu()`.
nodes.code_summary: The code uses a DINOv2 ViT-Large backbone (frozen) via timm to extract features from 518x518 aerial cactus images. A custom classifier head with residual blocks and batch normalization is trained on top of the frozen features. A 5-fold stratified split is used for validation, with training performed using BCEWithLogitsLoss, AdamW optimizer, cosine annealing scheduler with warmup, and mixed precision training. The feature extraction function attempts to concatenate cls and patch tokens from forward_features output, which caused the error.

nodes.plan: The issue is that the DINOv3 model is loaded from a local directory and checkpoint that doesn't exist. The fix is to use a simpler, more reliable approach: use a lightweight CNN backbone (like a small ResNet) that's available in PyTorch's `torchvision.models`, or use a pretrained model from `timm` without needing local files. Since we have internet access during development, we can directly download the model. I'll replace the DINOv3 approach with a standard pretrained ResNet50 backbone, which is available by default in PyTorch and doesn't require any manual file downloads.

nodes.plan: Looking at the error, the issue is clear: `test_ids_loaded` is collected from the test loader but when using multiple data loading workers with shuffling and batching, the tuple of IDs from the test loader isn't correctly accumulated as a flat list. The bug is that `test_ids_loaded` is reset in each fold, and during the first fold, it captures the last batch's IDs (not all IDs), causing a length mismatch with `test_predictions`. The fix: Instead of collecting `test_ids_loaded` inside the fold loop (which only keeps the last batch), we should collect all test IDs once before the fold loop from the test_loader, since the test set is fixed and doesn't change across folds. Let me provide the fix:
nodes.code_summary: The code loads Aerial Cactus images using PIL and applies stratified 5-fold cross-validation. Training uses augmentations (RandomHorizontalFlip, RandomRotation, ColorJitter, RandomResizedCrop) plus CutMix with 50% probability per batch. The model is EfficientNet-B0 (from timm) with a custom classifier head (linear layer to 1 output) and BCEWithLogitsLoss. Training uses AdamW optimizer, mixed precision (AMP), a warmup + cosine annealing scheduler, and early stopping. Test predictions are averaged across all 5 folds for the final submission.

Each worker loads full-resolution images and applies transforms (Resize to 224x224, RandomHorizontalFlip, etc.), which consumes significant shared memory per worker. **Fix**: Reduce `num_workers` to 0 (use main process only) and remove `pin_memory=True` for the image-loading DataLoaders. nodes.plan: Looking at the error, the issue is clear. The custom classifier head in `CactusClassifier` incorrectly uses `nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1)` followed by `nn.Flatten()` which produces a 1-dimensional output per image (not 1280). The original EfficientNet-V2-S already has a classifier that includes `nn.Dropout` and `nn.Linear(in_features, 1)`, and it uses average pooling internally before the classifier. The fix: Remove the custom `nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1)` and `nn.Flatten()` from the classifier, and simply replace the final `nn.Linear(1280, 1000)` with `nn.Linear(1280, 1)` followed by keeping the existing dropout.

It uses a pretrained EfficientNet-V2-S with a modified binary classification head. Training uses differential learning rates (backbone: 2e-5, classifier: 2e-4), AdamW optimizer, cosine annealing scheduler, mixed precision (AMP), gradient clipping, and early stopping with patience of 10. Evaluation metric is ROC AUC.

The fix: Remove the GeM pooling head (which introduces instability), simplify to a single classification head with standard global pooling, and remove the problematic `RandomErasing` augmentation. Also add gradient clipping to prevent divergence.

nodes.plan: Looking at the error, the root cause is clear: the DataLoader workers crash due to insufficient shared memory (`shm`). This is a common issue when using `num_workers>0` with `pin_memory=True` in environments with limited shared memory (like some Docker containers). The fix: Set `num_workers=0` to avoid multi-process data loading that uses shared memory. This is a minimal targeted fix that preserves the full solution intent and all model functionality. Since validation AUC already reached 1.0, the model performance will not be affected.
nodes.code_summary: The code implements a Vision Transformer (ViT) binary classifier for cactus detection. Data preprocessing includes stratified train/validation split (85/15), ImageNet normalization, and aggressive augmentation (random flips, rotation, color jitter). The model uses a timm vit_base_patch16_224 backbone with the last 6 transformer blocks unfrozen plus a custom MLP classifier head. Training uses differential learning rates (1e-5 backbone, 3e-4 head), AdamW optimizer, cosine annealing scheduler, gradient scaling for mixed precision, and MixUp augmentation. Validation strategy includes early stopping (patience 7) and test-time augmentation (horizontal flip averaging) for both validation and test inference.

nodes.code_summary: The code loads cactus image data and extracts handcrafted features including color histograms, GLCM texture features, LBP features, edge features, statistical features, HOG features, and pooled grayscale features. It also loads a DINOv3 Vision Transformer model for deep feature extraction, combines handcrafted and DINOv3 features, scales them with StandardScaler, and trains a simple MLP classifier with batch normalization and dropout. Validation uses stratified 5-fold cross-validation with ROC-AUC as the metric, and the model is trained with BCEWithLogitsLoss, AdamW optimizer, cosine annealing scheduler, and early stopping.

nodes.code_summary: The implementation uses EfficientNet-B3 as the backbone (fully trainable) with a binary classifier head for cactus detection. Data preprocessing includes ImageNet normalization, random horizontal flip, rotation, color jitter, and random erasing for augmentation. A progressive resizing strategy is employed, starting at 160px with batch size 64, then 192px with batch size 48, and finally 224px with batch size 32. The model is trained with BCEWithLogitsLoss, AdamW optimizer, linear warmup for 3 epochs followed by cosine annealing scheduler, and mixed precision training via GradScaler. Validation uses AUC with a stratified 85/15 train/val split, and test-time augmentation (original + horizontal flip) is applied for final predictions.

nodes.plan: Looking at the error, the issue is in the `extract_features` function. The DINOv2 model's `forward_features` returns the CLS token already as a 2D tensor (batch_size, feature_dim), so calling `.unsqueeze(1)` on it causes an IndexError. The patch tokens are 3D tensors. I need to fix the feature extraction to use the CLS token directly without modification. Additionally, I need to ensure batch normalization works correctly during training by setting `model.train()` for the classifier head (which is the only part being trained - it's fine). Let me fix the extract_features function:
nodes.code_summary: The code loads a pretrained DINOv2 large model (vit_large_patch14_dinov2.lvd142m) via timm with the classifier head removed. The backbone is frozen and a custom classification head (with residual connections, batch norm, dropout, and GELU activations) is trained on top. Data preprocessing includes resizing to 518x518, random horizontal/vertical flips, and ColorJitter augmentations. The training uses BCEWithLogitsLoss, AdamW optimizer, cosine learning rate scheduler with warmup, mixed precision training (GradScaler/autocast), and early stopping with patience of 7 epochs. Validation is done using ROC AUC score on a stratified 5-fold split (first fold used). The bug is that the code tries to access output["x_norm_clstoken"] from model.forward_features() but the actual output is a raw tensor, not a dictionary.

nodes.code_summary: The pipeline loads cactus image data (train/test splits), uses a CactusDataset class with augmentations (horizontal flip, rotation, color jitter), an EfficientNet-B0 backbone with a modified first convolutional layer (stride=1, padding=0) for 32x32 inputs, and a linear classifier head with dropout. It uses 3-fold StratifiedKFold cross-validation with AdamW optimizer, cosine annealing scheduler, label smoothing, gradient clipping, and early stopping. Test-time augmentation (10 stochastic transforms) is applied per fold, and predictions are combined via geometric mean across folds.

nodes.code_summary: The code loads leaf data (tabular margin/shape/texture features + images) and performs a train/validation split (712/179). Tabular features are engineered via per-group statistics (mean, std, min, max, skew, kurtosis, quartiles, IQR, range, CV), ratio features, cross-group correlations, per-group PCA (8 components), and difference PCA (5 components), all fitted on the train fold only. Image features (1152-dim) are extracted using a pretrained SigLIP2 model (google/siglip2-so400m-patch16-256). Combined features (1236-dim) are fed into a 3-layer MLP with BatchNorm, GELU, and dropout. The model is trained for up to 200 epochs with AdamW, cosine annealing scheduler, label smoothing (0.1), mixed precision, and early stopping (patience 30). The final validation log loss is reported. The model is then retrained on the full dataset and used to generate test predictions for submission.

nodes.plan: The CUDA initialization error occurs because the validation DataLoader is created inside the training loop with GPU tensors already on device, causing issues with multiprocessing workers trying to access the same GPU. The fix is to validate using the main thread without separate workers, or to keep tensors on CPU and move to device per batch. Additionally, I see structural issues: the `test_loader` uses `TensorDataset` with a single tensor but `(batch_X,)` unpacking, and the feature dimension 328 is not divisible by 3 for the multi-branch network. Let me fix all bugs systematically.
nodes.code_summary: The code implements a multi-class leaf classification solution using a PyTorch multi-branch neural network with attention. Feature engineering includes statistical aggregations (mean, std, skew, kurtosis, etc.) per feature type (margin, shape, texture), PCA, RobustScaler normalization, interaction features, and target encoding via binning. The model is a MultiBranchLeafNet that splits features into 3 branches (each with Linear-BatchNorm-LeakyReLU-Dropout blocks), applies multi-head cross-attention, then fusion and classification layers. Training uses CrossEntropyLoss with label smoothing, AdamW optimizer, CosineAnnealingWarmRestarts scheduler, early stopping, and gradient clipping.
nodes.analysis: The execution failed due to a shape mismatch error in the neural network during training. The MultiBranchLeafNet model splits the input features into 3 branches, but the input dimension (328) is not evenly divisible by 3, causing a mismatch where one branch gets 110 features while the branch's linear layer expects 109 features (328//3 = 109.33, floor division gives 109). The error occurred at the first Linear layer of branch1 where a tensor of shape (32, 110) was multiplied by weight of shape (109, 128).

The fix is to validate using the main thread without separate workers, or to keep tensors on CPU and move to device per batch. Additionally, I see structural issues: the `test_loader` uses `TensorDataset` with a single tensor but `(batch_X,)` unpacking, and the feature dimension 328 is not divisible by 3 for the multi-branch network. Let me fix all bugs systematically.
The code implements a multi-class leaf classification solution using a PyTorch multi-branch neural network with attention. Feature engineering includes statistical aggregations (mean, std, skew, kurtosis, etc.) per feature type (margin, shape, texture), PCA, RobustScaler normalization, interaction features, and target encoding via binning. The model is a MultiBranchLeafNet that splits features into 3 branches (each with Linear-BatchNorm-LeakyReLU-Dropout blocks), applies multi-head cross-attention, then fusion and classification layers. Training uses CrossEntropyLoss with label smoothing, A...
The execution failed due to a shape mismatch error in the neural network during training. The MultiBranchLeafNet model splits the input features into 3 branches, but the input dimension (328) is not evenly divisible by 3, causing a mismatch where one branch gets 110 features while the branch's linear layer expects 109 features (328//3 = 109.33, floor division gives 109). The error occurred at the first Linear layer of branch1 where a tensor of shape (32, 110) was multiplied by weight of shape (109, 128).

nodes.plan: Looking at the error, the root cause is clear: the `MultiBranchLeafNet.forward()` method pads the input to a multiple of 3, but the branch sub-networks are initialized with `input_dim // 3` which doesn't account for padding. When `n_features=328` (not divisible by 3), padding rounds up to 330, but each branch is initialized with `328//3=109` while actually receiving `330//3=110` features. The fix is to compute the branch size dynamically at initialization time, ensuring it matches what each branch will actually receive after padding.
nodes.code_summary: The code implements a leaf classification pipeline using tabular feature engineering (per-row statistics, PCA, robust scaling, cross-feature interactions, diff features, variance threshold filtering), target encoding via binning with stratified k-fold, and a MultiBranchLeafNet neural network with 3 branches, multi-head cross-attention, batch normalization, dropout, and label smoothing. Validation uses a stratified 5-fold split with early stopping, and the metric is log loss (lower is better).
nodes.analysis: The execution failed due to a KeyError when trying to assign the 'margin_skew' column in the feature engineering function. The error occurs because `np.mean((X_cur - mean_vals) ** 3, axis=1)` returns a 2D array (891, 891) instead of a 1D array, which occurs when `mean_vals` has shape (891, 1) and `X_cur` has shape (891, 64), leading to broadcasting producing an unintended large array. The code crashed before any model training could begin.

nodes.plan: I'll analyze the error and fix it. The root cause is that `torch.hub.load()` with `source="local"` is trying to find a local directory `./working/torch_hub/dinov3-main/` that doesn't exist. Since we have internet access during code development, I should use the standard torch.hub.load with a GitHub repository reference instead. The fix is to use `torch.hub.load('facebookresearch/dinov2', 'dinov2_vitl14')` or similar, which will download the model from the internet during development. Let me also note that the sample_submission.csv has 99 rows and 100 columns, and the test.csv has 99 rows. The training data has 891 rows.

nodes.code_summary: The solution uses a multi-model ensemble with 5-fold StratifiedKFold cross-validation. Feature engineering creates cross-features (differences, ratios, statistics, entropy) from margin/shape/texture groups, applies PCA dimensionality reduction, and generates polynomial interaction features. Three models are trained per fold: (1) XGBoost on scaled tabular features, (2) a 4-layer MLP with GELU activations and batch normalization on SigLIP2 vision transformer image embeddings with Gaussian noise augmentation, (3) Logistic Regression with polynomial features and PCA reduction, calibrated with isotonic regression. Predictions are ensembled via weighted averaging with weights optimized on OOF predictions using log-loss.

The training loss is around 1.5 while validation loss is about 1.07, indicating severe overfitting on the small dataset (891 samples). Historical successful experiments show that gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost) on well-engineered tabular features consistently achieve good performance with less overfitting, while complex neural networks with image embeddings often overfit or require extensive regularization. Failed experiments deviated from the plan or used overly complex multi-stage training. Therefore, I propose to replace the entire neural network with an XGBoost classifier on engineered tabular features (mirroring successful historical experiments) and add a li...
nodes.code_summary: The code loads leaf image and tabular data (margin, shape, texture features), engineers extensive features including per-group statistics, polynomial/interaction features, and PCA components, then applies feature selection. It defines a 5-fold cross-validation ensemble combining XGBoost on tabular features and a fine-tuned EfficientNet-B0 on images, with a logistic regression meta-learner to blend predictions. The metric is multi-class log loss, which is lower-is-better.
nodes.analysis: The script crashed with a ValueError due to unpacking mismatch. The `engineer_features` function was defined twice (once incorrectly with 3 return values, then later correctly with 3 return values), but the first call to process `val_set` used `fit_scalers=scaler_obj` and expected 2 return values (`X_val_feat, _`), while the function at that point in the code (the first definition) returns 3 values when `fit_scalers` is not None, causing a "too many values to unpack" error. The execution stopped before any model training or metric computation could occur.

nodes.code_summary: The code loads tabular leaf features (margin, shape, texture) and images, then engineers tabular features including statistical summaries (mean, std, skew, kurtosis, quantiles, CV), ratio features, cross-group correlations, and PCA per group and on differences. Image features are extracted using a pretrained SigLIP2 vision model. All features are concatenated and fed into a 3-layer MLP classifier with BatchNorm, GELU activations, and dropout. Training uses a two-stage approach: Stage 1 trains the MLP head (frozen SigLIP2) with AdamW and cosine annealing, and Stage 2 continues with a lower learning rate. The best model is selected based on validation log loss. Finally, the model is retrained on the full dataset and predictions are generated for the test set.

nodes.code_summary: The code implements a multi-modal ensemble for leaf species classification (99 classes). Data preprocessing includes loading tabular features (margin, shape, texture - each with 64 attributes) and images. Feature engineering creates cross-feature differences/ratios, statistical summaries (mean, std, skew, kurtosis), PCA reductions per feature group and globally, polynomial features, and high-variance polynomial expansions. Three models are trained in 5-fold stratified cross-validation: (1) XGBoost on tabular features, (2) a multi-layer perceptron with batch normalization and GELU activation on SigLIP2 image embeddings with noisy augmentation, and (3) multinomial logistic regression with polynomial features and PCA reduction, calibrated via isotonic regression. Predictions are ensembled via weighted averaging with weights optimized on out-of-fold log-loss.

nodes.code_summary: The code uses a multi-modal approach combining tabular features (margin, shape, texture) reduced via per-group PCA (32 components each), and SigLIP2 image features (1152-dim) further reduced via PCA to 128 components. These are concatenated and feature-selected using SelectKBest with mutual information (k=150). A stratified 85/15 train-validation split is used. The ensemble consists of XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost classifiers with Platt calibration, plus a stacking meta-learner (LogisticRegression) trained on 5-fold out-of-fold predictions from the base models. Final predictions blend averaged calibrated probabilities with meta-learner probabilities (50/50). Validation uses multiclass log loss.

nodes.code_summary: The code implements a multi-branch neural network (MultiBranchLeafNet) for leaf species classification. Feature engineering includes per-row statistics (mean, std, skew, kurtosis, etc.) for margin/shape/texture features, PCA reduction, RobustScaler normalization, cross-feature interactions, and difference features. Target encoding via binning with stratified 5-fold cross-validation is also added. The model has 3 parallel branches followed by multi-head cross-attention and a fusion classifier. Training uses AdamW optimizer, cosine annealing warm restarts, label smoothing, gradient clipping, and early stopping with validation log loss as the metric.

nodes.code_summary: The code implements a multi-modal leaf classification pipeline combining tabular features and image features. Data preprocessing: stratified train/validation split by species, extensive tabular feature engineering (raw values, statistical moments, polynomial and interaction features, PCA projections with StandardScaler). Images are preprocessed via ResNet-style transforms and DINOv2 ViT-L/14 extracts 1024-d embeddings. Model architecture: separate projectors for tabular (512-d) and image (512-d) features, bidirectional multi-head cross-attention fusion, LayerNorm + FFN, concatenated 1024-d fused representation, then a 3-layer MLP classifier with label smoothing cross-entropy loss, AdamW optimizer with cosine annealing schedule, and mixed-precision training. Validation metric: multiclass log loss.

The final validation score was 0.01437, indicating high classification performance on the leaf species classification task. The submission file was saved with 99 species columns.

nodes.plan: Looking at the error, the issue is clear: In the forward pass, `final_features = torch.cat([fused, tab_proj, img_proj], dim=1)` creates a tensor of size 2048 (1024 from fused + 512 + 512), but the classifier expects 1536 dimensions. The fix is to remove the redundant concatenation of `tab_proj` and `img_proj` since `fused` already contains cross-attended versions of both. We'll just use `fused` directly (1024 dims) and update the classifier input dimension accordingly.
nodes.code_summary: The code loads leaf image and tabular (margin, shape, texture) data from CSV files, performs stratified train/validation split, and engineers extensive tabular features including raw features, per-group statistics (mean, std, skew, kurtosis, entropy), cross-group interactions, and PCA projections standardized with StandardScaler. Images are resized, center-cropped, and normalized using standard ImageNet statistics, then DINOv2 ViT-L/14 extracts 1024-dimensional image features. The model is a multi-modal classifier: tabular features go through a 3-layer MLP projector, image features through a 1-layer MLP projector, followed by bidirectional cross-attention fusion (8-head) and a final classifier head with label smoothing (0.1). Training uses AdamW, cosine annealing LR scheduler, mixed precision (AMP), and early stopping with patience of 50 on validation log loss.

The issue is **data leakage through image feature extraction**. **Root Cause Analysis:** The critical bug is that `extract_image_features()` uses the SigLIP2 model `model_siglip` which is a global variable. When Stage 2 fine-tuning updates `model_siglip` weights, this affects the subsequent call to `extract_image_features(train_ids)` for the full training set. However, the test predictions are generated using features extracted BEFORE Stage 2 fine-tuning of the retraining phase. This creates a mismatch between features used for training and inference. But more fundamentally, the validation score of 0.1091 is suspiciously good for a 99-class problem with only 712 training samples and a simple MLP head. This sugges...
nodes.code_summary: The code implements a leaf classification pipeline combining engineered tabular features (statistical summaries, ratios, correlations, PCA per feature group) with image features extracted from SigLIP2 (google/siglip2-so400m-patch16-256). A train/validation split is performed using StratifiedKFold. A fully connected MLP classifier (LeafClassifier) with 3 hidden layers, BatchNorm, GELU activation, and dropout is trained in two stages, both with SigLIP2 frozen. Stage 1 uses a higher learning rate (1e-3), Stage 2 uses a lower learning rate (5e-4). The model is trained using cross-entropy loss with label smoothing, mixed precision (AMP), cosine annealing scheduler, and early stopping based on validation log loss. After validation, the model is retrained on the full dataset and used to generate test predictions.

The code then tries to call it with only `pixel_values`, causing the error. The fix is to use `AutoModel.from_pretrained(..., attn_implementation="eager")` and pass through the vision model directly, or alternatively load `AutoModel` and call `model_siglip.vision_model(pixel_values=batch)` to get vision-only outputs. I'll use the latter approach since hooks are already attached to vision_model layers. Also, there are duplicate sections (DataLoaders and model initialization) that will cause variable overwriting — I'll remove the redundant blocks.

The original CatBoost model was defined with `random_seed=42`, and then `clf.set_params(random_state=42+fold)` adds `random_state`, causing a conflict. The fix: remove `random_seed` from the original CatBoost definition, keeping only `random_state`, so the cloned models don't have the conflict.

It performs image feature extraction using a SigLIP2 vision model via HuggingFace transformers. After a stratified train/validation split, it applies per-group PCA on tabular features (margin, shape, texture separately), standard scaling, PCA on image features, and SelectKBest with mutual information for feature selection. A stacking ensemble is built using calibrated XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost models as base learners, with out-of-fold predictions feeding into a logistic regression meta-learner. Validation uses a blend of averaged calibrated probabilities and meta-learner predictions, evaluated by multi-class log loss.

nodes.code_summary: Data preprocessing: outlier removal based on fare amount, passenger count, and NYC coordinate bounds. Feature engineering: temporal features (hour, month, dayofweek with cyclical encoding, rush hour/night/weekend flags), spatial features (Haversine distance, Manhattan distance, bearing, center coordinates, airport/manhattan proximity), and location-based group statistics (mean/median fare by rounded lat/lon). Model: two-stage XGBoost with DMatrix format — Stage 1 trains on log1p-transformed fare (RMSE objective, early stopping), Stage 2 trains on residuals from Stage 1. Final predictions are the sum of both stages, clipped at $0.50 minimum. Validation: RMSE on a time-based 80/20 split.
nodes.analysis: ⚠️ DATA LEAKAGE DETECTED (Confidence: HIGH) The code has a data leakage issue in the `extract_group_stats` function. This function computes group statistics (mean, std, count of `fare_amount`) grouped by rounded pickup location coordinates from the **entire training set**, then merges these statistics back into both the training and test sets. However, the validation set is carved from the training set AFTER these statistics are computed, meaning the validation data's location-based fare statistics are influenced by the validation data itself (since the statistics were computed on the full training set before the train/val split). This is a form of target leakage — the model sees global location-based fare averages during training that incorporate information from what will become the validation set, leading to an artificially low validation RMSE. nodes.code_summary: The code preprocesses NYC taxi trip data by cleaning outliers (coordinate bounds, fare range, passenger count), engineers temporal features (hour, day, weekday, rush hour indicators), distance features (haversine, Manhattan, bearing), and location-aware features (distances to JFK/LGA/Manhattan, grid cell encodings). Features are scaled using RobustScaler and split temporally (80/20). Two models are trained: (1) a GeoAwareNN with geographic embedding layers that discretize lat/lon into grid cells, batch normalization, dropout, and Huber loss, trained with AdamW and learning rate scheduling; (2) an XGBoost regressor with tuned hyperparameters and early stopping. Predictions are ensemble-weighted (0.3 NN, 0.7 XGB), clipped to [$1, $500], and saved as a submission CSV.

nodes.plan: Looking at the error, the issue is that `categorical_feature` in LightGBM's parameters is passed as feature names, but the data is provided as numpy arrays (via `.values`). LightGBM needs either column indices when using numpy arrays, or requires prefix "name:" for column names when using a pandas DataFrame. The fix: Remove the `categorical_feature` entry from model_params dict (since we're passing numpy arrays), and instead pass it as a list of column indices to `lgb.Dataset` call using the `categorical_feature` parameter there. This way LightGBM will interpret them as column indices correctly.

nodes.code_summary: The code implements a LightGBM regression model for NYC taxi fare prediction. Preprocessing includes filtering invalid coordinates and fare outliers. Feature engineering extracts temporal features (hour, day, month, weekend, rush hour flags), spatial features (Haversine distance, Manhattan distance, bearing, airport distances, grid zone IDs), interaction features (hour-distance, zone pairs), and log-transformed zone frequency counts. Validation uses a 80/20 stratified split by fare bins with RMSE as the evaluation metric. The failure occurred because string-typed categorical features were included in a NumPy array passed to lgb.Dataset, which cannot handle string data.

nodes.code_summary: The code loads NYC taxi fare data (labels.csv and test.csv), cleans it by filtering coordinates within NYC bounds and removing invalid fares/passenger counts, then engineers features including temporal features (hour, day, month, rush hour flags), distance features (Haversine distance, Manhattan distance, bearing), and location features (distances to airports and Manhattan, NYC boundary flags). A LightGBM regression model is trained with stratified train/validation split (80/20) using fare bins for stratification, with early stopping (50 rounds patience) over 2000 boosting rounds. Validation RMSE is used as the evaluation metric, and test predictions are saved to a submission CSV.

The key issue is NOT in the augmentation itself but in the **temporal split being performed BEFORE the augmentation**, ensuring no validation data leaks into training. nodes.title: Use EfficientNet-B0 with end-to-end fine-tuning and CutMix augmentation for cactus classification
nodes.action: Use a pretrained EfficientNet-B0 backbone from timm, fine-tune end-to-end with BCEWithLogitsLoss, AdamW optimizer (backbone lr=5e-5, head lr=1e-3), warmup cosine annealing scheduler, CutMix augmentation (50% probability per batch), gradient clipping, and early stopping based on validation AUC.
applies_when: When performing binary image classification on the aerial cactus identification dataset with limited data (~14K images) and near-perfect validation AUC is desired.

nodes.title: Use EfficientNet-B3 with progressive resizing for improved generalization
nodes.action: Use a pretrained EfficientNet-B3 backbone with progressive resizing (start at 160px, then 192px, then 224px) with corresponding batch sizes (64, 48, 32). Train with BCEWithLogitsLoss, AdamW optimizer, linear warmup for 3 epochs followed by cosine annealing, CutMix augmentation, and early stopping. Use test-time augmentation (horizontal flip averaging) for final predictions.
applies_when: When aiming for near-perfect validation AUC (>0.9999) on aerial cactus identification and wanting to reduce overfitting through curriculum learning on image resolution.

nodes.title: Use ConvNeXt-Tiny backbone with CutMix and MixUp for strong regularization
nodes.action: Use a pretrained ConvNeXt-Tiny backbone from timm with a custom MLP classifier head. Apply CutMix (25% probability) and MixUp (25% probability) augmentations. Use AdamW optimizer with differential learning rates (backbone 5e-5, head 1e-3), warmup cosine annealing scheduler, label smoothing BCE loss, gradient clipping, and early stopping.
applies_when: When the current model (e.g., EfficientNet-B4) shows signs of overfitting (perfect validation AUC but compressed test predictions) and a stronger regularization approach is needed.

nodes.title: Use EfficientNet-B4 with CBAM attention and MixUp/CutMix for best performance
nodes.action: Use a pretrained EfficientNet-B4 backbone with a custom CBAM attention head and 3-layer MLP classifier. Apply RandAugment, RandomErasing, MixUp (80% probability), and CutMix (25% probability) augmentations. Train with Focal Loss with label smoothing, AdamW optimizer, OneCycleLR scheduler, mixed precision, and early stopping. Use test-time augmentation (horizontal flip) for final predictions.
applies_when: When aiming for the highest possible validation AUC (1.0) on aerial cactus identification and computational resources allow for a larger model.

nodes.title: Use Vision Transformer (ViT) with partial unfreezing and MixUp for cactus classification
nodes.action: Use a pretrained ViT-Base/16 backbone from timm, unfreeze the last 6 transformer blocks, and add a custom MLP classifier head. Apply MixUp augmentation (50% probability). Use differential learning rates (backbone 1e-5, head 3e-4), AdamW optimizer, cosine annealing scheduler, mixed precision, and early stopping. Use test-time augmentation (horizontal flip averaging) for final predictions.
applies_when: When wanting to leverage Vision Transformer architectures for aerial cactus identification with moderate computational resources.

nodes.action: Use a frozen pretrained backbone (e.g., EfficientNet-B0, ResNet50) to extract features, cache them to disk, then train a small MLP classifier (LayerNorm + 2-3 linear layers with GELU and dropout) on the extracted features using BCEWithLogitsLoss, AdamW optimizer, and ReduceLROnPlateau scheduler.
applies_when: When needing a quick baseline or when computational resources are limited (e.g., GPU memory constraints) for aerial cactus identification.
